cap.n0: Grow a model's dictionary,|and it gains almost 700 million parameters.
cap.n1: Before it has learned a thing.|From 32,000 entries to 200,000.|Where do they all come from?
cap.n2: That dictionary is the vocabulary:|every token the model knows, a word or a piece of a word.|Last episode's card catalogue, one drawer per entry.
cap.n3: This is Lecture 1 of Professor Yufei|Ding's CSE 291P at UC San Diego.
cap.n4: Her slide 20. Llama 1 and 2, 2023: 32,000 entries.|Llama 3, 2024: about 128,000.
cap.n5: GPT-4o's tokenizer, 2024: about 200,000.|Different families, one direction:|vocabularies keep growing.
cap.c4: So I hope you can discuss with your classmates|and try to think about|what is the strength of large vocabulary|and what is the weakness of large vocabulary.
cap.n6: Strength first.|Why would a bigger vocabulary make a model smarter?
cap.n7: A bigger catalogue has room for bigger pieces:|more meaning per token.
cap.n8: Take the word vocabulary.|Llama 2 cuts it into 4 pieces.|Llama 3 keeps it as 1 token.
cap.c1: And usually like the larger vocabulary means that you|can encode the same meaning using less number of tokens.|And less number of tokens also means like it's cheaper.
cap.n9: Fewer tokens per page: more pages fit in the context window,|the text a model can take in at once.
cap.n10: Her slide 22 says a book would take three|times the space with 32,000 entries. Not three times.
cap.n11: Same texts, both tokenizers:|we measured about 12 percent fewer tokens on English novels,|and about 21 percent fewer on Python code.
cap.n12: Her slide also says a big vocabulary makes 1000 one token.|Not quite: Llama 2 splits it into four digits.
cap.n13: Llama 3 and GPT-4o's tokenizer cut it into 100, then 0.|That cut is a design choice, not a matter of size.
cap.n14: Now, heavier. Reason one: open any drawer,|and inside is a long strip of numbers.
cap.n15: Every entry gets its own row of numbers.|The row's length is the model's width, its hidden size.|At a width of 4,096, that is 4,096 numbers per entry.
cap.n16: Together the rows make the embedding matrix,|the table at the model's input.|Each number in it is a parameter the model must learn.
cap.n17: Her slide 23 multiplies it out.|32,000 entries times 4,096: about 131 million.
cap.n18: 200,000 entries at the same width: about 819 million.
cap.n19: 688 million more, in the input table alone.|Almost 700 million, and every one starts untrained.
cap.n20: That's where they come from:|one long strip for every new drawer.
cap.n21: Reason two: the output layer, the model's last step.|For every token it writes,|the model scores every entry in its vocabulary.
cap.n22: Picture a clerk who must tick every drawer in the wall,|for every single token.
cap.c7: So that generation, the last layer,|the computation cost is proportional to|the number of the size of the vocabulary.
cap.n23: Same two numbers, now as work:|about 131 million multiply-adds per token at 32,000 entries,|about 819 million at 200,000.
cap.n24: Reason three: data.|A bigger vocabulary has more rare entries,|and a rare entry is seen less often in training.
cap.n25: A drawer that's hardly ever opened gathers dust.
cap.c9: But it's fine today because we have a lot of data.|So that is no longer a big issue, but it used to be,
cap.n26: One honest limit. A 2024 study still found under-trained|entries in every model it tested:|typically 0.1 to 1 percent of the vocabulary.
cap.n27: Now the bill.|As she said, fewer tokens is cheaper: chat APIs take text,|not token IDs, but the bill is counted in tokens.
cap.n28: It's a post office that charges by weight.|So weigh the parcel at home:|count the tokens on your own machine first.
cap.n29: Her slide 24 has rules of thumb for 1,000 characters.|English: about 250 tokens.
cap.n30: Code: not 500 to 750.|On today's tokenizers we measured 224 to 340,|about the same as English.
cap.n31: And 1,000 digits: 334 tokens on GPT-4o's tokenizer,|about 1,000 on Llama 2's.|Rules of thumb vary by tokenizer: count with the real one.
cap.c11: it's better to do some cost analysis.
cap.n32: So the course worksheet does one.|A research paper of about 10,000 tokens,|five questions, answers of 300 tokens.
cap.n33: The prices on the course worksheet:|$1.75 per million tokens in, $14 per million out.
cap.n34: The naive way sends the whole paper with every question:|about 2 cents a question.|Five questions: about 11 cents.
cap.n35: Or let the post office keep a copy of the paper.|That's a cache.
cap.c13: the cache input is only one-tenth|of their uncached input price,
cap.n36: On this price list,|the first question pays full price for the paper,|and the next four pay a tenth.|Total: about 4.6 cents.
cap.n37: Or send less: retrieval.|Cut the paper into 20 chunks of 500 tokens,|and send only the 3 most relevant: 1,500 tokens a question.
cap.n39: Retrieval, at 3.4 cents, beats the cache.|Always? Fetch 6 chunks instead of 3, and caching wins.
cap.c14c: but sometimes one is better,|sometimes the other one is better.
cap.n40: So a bigger dictionary packs more meaning into each token.|But it is paid for three times: a strip in every drawer,|a score for every drawer at every step,|and data for the rare ones.
cap.n41: And every call is billed in tokens. Count them first.
cap.n42: Every drawer now has a score.|Next: how does the model pick one?
